subject: Atlantic Bank - private access channel recommendation
messages:
From: James Park <j.park@atlanticbank.com>
To: marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com
Date: 2027-05-01 13:12 -04:00
Subject: Atlantic Bank — connecting Redwood Private

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for taking this. We're evaluating Redwood Private for a production LLM that will live in our AWS account and process payment-related PII. Our network operations ask for a short recommendation on three access patterns: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site (S2S) VPN. Key constraints:
- No internet egress from model traffic (must stay on private backbone).
- PCI/DSS + SOC2 compliance; auditability and flow logs required.
- Primary deployment in AWS us-east-1; we also have an on-prem primary datacenter in Boston and several branch offices that will call the service indirectly.
- Target 10 ms RTT for token latency across our application servers and Redwood hosts.

I've attached our current topology diagram (network-diagram-v1.pdf). Can you outline pros/cons and the operational trade-offs for each option and suggest a recommended path? We're aiming to pick an approach this week so we can budget for a PoC.

Appreciate it — James
Senior Cloud Architect
Atlantic Bank

Attachment: network-diagram-v1.pdf

From: marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com
To: James Park <j.park@atlanticbank.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com, lauren_bishop@redwoodinference.com
Date: 2027-05-01 14:05 -04:00
Subject: Re: Atlantic Bank — connecting Redwood Private

Hi James — thanks for the context and the diagram. High level guidance up front, then we can dive into specifics in a short call:

Summary recommendation (short):
- Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) from your VPC to our private service endpoints for PCI/SOC2 workloads.
- Supplement: S2S VPN from on-prem branches into that VPC (or direct connect if you prefer predictable bandwidth) for branch traffic.
- Avoid: Relying solely on VPC peering for cross-account access unless you already have non-overlapping CIDRs and strong network isolation policies; peering can blur ownership boundaries and complicate firewalling.

Why PrivateLink first?
- Traffic never transits the public internet and stays within AWS private networking.
- Interface endpoints give fine-grained control over which services are reachable (security + auditability).
- Easier to support per-account IAM and endpoint policies; fewer route table changes required on your side.

Tradeoffs to call out:
- Latency: PrivateLink will generally meet your 10 ms requirement inside a single AZ/region; cross-AZ may add a few ms. We'll validate during PoC.
- Throughput: Interface endpoints have bandwidth limits per ENI — we'll size and recommend placement.
- Operational: Requires creation of interface endpoints in your VPC and an accept step on our side; we provide step-by-step.

When VPC peering makes sense:
- If you need extremely low latency between large fleets inside your VPC and our hosts and you control both sides' routing policies, peering is simpler. But peering exposes subnets across accounts and needs non-overlapping CIDR ranges.

When S2S VPN fits:
- Good for branch offices or datacenter fallback; lower cost but variable latency/jitter vs direct connect. Use VPN to reach your VPC that hosts the PrivateLink endpoints.

Next requests from our side to produce a concrete architecture and PoC plan:
1) Confirm your VPC CIDR(s) and whether you use overlapping IPs across accounts/AZs.
2) Who on your network team will accept endpoint connection requests (ops@atlanticbank.com OK?).
3) Expected QPS and max token throughput so we can size endpoints.

I've attached a short summary (redwood-connectivity-options-summary.pdf) and will pull Karthik in for a technical walkthrough. Available slot: Friday 10:00 AM ET for a 30-min technical review.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Enterprise Solutions Lead | Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood-connectivity-options-summary.pdf

From: James Park <j.park@atlanticbank.com>
To: marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com
Date: 2027-05-01 16:22 -04:00
Subject: Re: Atlantic Bank — connecting Redwood Private

Hi Marissa — thanks, that level of detail is helpful. A few clarifications:
- Our VPC CIDR in us-east-1 is 10.10.0.0/16 (single account). We also have an on-prem range 172.16.0.0/16. Branch offices NAT behind a set of egress IPs.
- We cannot allow any model traffic to traverse the public internet — all egress must be within our VPC or through our VPN tunnels.
- We currently do not have Direct Connect and the ops team prefers VPN for initial PoC.
- QPS: average 25 qps, burst to 150 qps; tokens per request ~400.

Attaching a quick topology note (topology-notes.docx). Ops will accept endpoint requests at ops@atlanticbank.com. Friday 10:00 ET works.

James

Attachment: topology-notes.docx

From: karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com
To: marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com, lauren_bishop@redwoodinference.com
Date: 2027-05-02 09:00 -04:00
Subject: Internal: Atlantic Bank access pattern appraisal

Team — internal technical read for the PoC and our recommended architecture. Summary: PrivateLink + customer VPN into customer VPC hosting endpoints. Details and operational notes below.

Notes:
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is the lowest-risk from an audit/compliance perspective because it keeps sovereignty of routing in the customer's account and avoids cross-account route propagation. Endpoint policies and VPC flow logs satisfy audit requirements.
- Peering: requires non-overlapping CIDRs (we have 10.11.0.0/16 used in our infra; if they had overlapping ranges we'd need NAT or proxy). Peering also means their route tables point to our subnets — increases blast radius and complicates firewall rules. Not preferred for PCI workloads unless strictly controlled.
- S2S VPN: good for on-prem and branch traffic; expect 5–30 ms additional latency depending on path. Jitter/bandwidth limits are a concern for bursts (we should document throttling/backpressure behavior in the SDK).

Sizing & availability:
- With 25 average QPS and 150 burst, we'll provision multiple ENIs across AZs for PrivateLink and enable cross-AZ ENI fallback. We'll provide a sizing table for ENI count and estimated per-hour cost.

Operational checklist for PoC (deliverables):
1) Customer: create interface endpoints in the VPC and share endpoint ids + ARNs.
2) Customer: open ops@atlanticbank.com to accept our service VPC association.
3) Redwood: deploy a dedicated Private service alias in us-east-1 and publish endpoint service name.
4) Joint: run latency/throughput tests, capture VPC flow logs and TLS termination proof for compliance.

Edge cases and fallbacks:
- If customer requires cross-account direct peering for ultra-low single-digit ms, we can explore peering in a dedicated peered account with strict AWS NACLs and explicit route filters, but this is more operationally heavy.
- For branches with poor connectivity, recommend local caching/proxying to reduce tokens per round-trip.

I'll prepare an architecture diagram and a mutual action plan. Tagging this as high priority for the PoC.

-Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

From: marissa_cole@redwoodinference.com
To: James Park <j.park@atlanticbank.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwoodinference.com, lauren_bishop@redwoodinference.com
Date: 2027-05-02 13:45 -04:00
Subject: Re: Atlantic Bank — connecting Redwood Private (next steps)

James — thanks for the quick responses and the topology notes. Pulling this together into an actionable plan:

Recommendation (final):
- PoC architecture: PrivateLink interface endpoints in your us-east-1 VPC + S2S VPN from your on-prem datacenter to that VPC. Redwood will publish a service name and accept endpoint connection requests.
- Why: balances compliance, auditability, and predictable private routing while allowing branches/on-prem to reach the endpoints without exposing traffic to the public internet.

Immediate next steps (mutual action plan attached):
1) You: create interface endpoints in the VPC (10.10.0.0/16) for the specified service and add ops@atlanticbank.com as the acceptance contact.
2) You: provide a contact for on-prem VPN engineers and the expected bandwidth for the VPN tunnels.
3) Redwood: publish service alias and send connection request; provision ENIs across AZs and provide a sizing + cost estimate.
4) Joint: 30-min test window to run 25 qps baseline and 150 qps burst with VPC flow logs enabled. Capture latency, packet loss, and TLS handshake metadata for compliance evidence.

I'll drop a calendar invite for Friday 10:00 ET. Attached: mutual-action-plan.xlsx and a short design sketch. I've also added the design doc to the shared drive: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1a2b3c4d-design-doc

If the ops team prefers Direct Connect later for predictable bandwidth, we can update the plan — VPN is fine for the PoC.

Talk Friday — Marissa
Enterprise Solutions Lead
Redwood Inference

Attachment: mutual-action-plan.xlsx
